article_title: Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance
citation: Dhanya Pramod and Kanchan Pranay Patil. (2026). Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02168-4
title: Integrated GDCT–SDT–SPT framework for agentic AI-supported online learning
description: The article proposes an integrated theoretical framework in which Holmberg's Guided Didactic Conversation Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Social Presence Theory are "viewed not as additive, but as interlinked theoretical approaches". GDCT forms the pedagogical and interactional layer explaining dialogue, guidance, feedback, and responsiveness; SDT explains how psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) relate to learning motivation; SPT explains how interactivity, information sharing, and collaboration form social presence. The two pathways converge at learner engagement, which relates to perceived learner performance.
requirements: Learners must have prior experience with AI-based online learning platforms for the perceived constructs to be meaningful
constraints: The framework was tested with perception-based survey data among Indian business-school students, not with an experimental system or objective performance measures
target_learners: business and management students in higher education (MBA, PGDM, BBA)
target_learning_goals: perceived learning performance in AI-supported online learning
examples: The conceptual framework (Fig. 1) positions perceived agentic AI affordances, psychological perceptions, motivational and social-relational mechanisms, engagement, and perceived performance in one structural model tested with PLS-SEM
key_sources: Dhanya Pramod and Kanchan Pranay Patil. (2026). Agentic AI in educational environments and its association with social and motivational pathways to learning performance. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-02168-4

article_title: Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement
citation: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1
title: Group disciplinary engagement (GDE) framework: engagement as collective, multidimensional, dynamic, and contextualized
description: The GDE framework conceptualizes engagement at the group rather than individual level, extending productive disciplinary engagement (Engle & Conant) with a situative perspective. The authors "define group's productive engagement as joint participation (behaviorally engaged) with a positive and inclusive interpersonal climate (socio-emotionally engaged), which together provide as an initial foundation to enable joint knowledge co-construction (collaborative engagement)", plus metacognitive and disciplinary engagement. Engagement is treated as co-negotiated norms unfolding dynamically over time and situated in curriculum, task, and instructional contexts.
requirements: Observational rubric ratings of group-level quality across five dimensions during collaborative activity
constraints: Developed for collaborative group activity in science, mathematics, and engineering units incorporating modeling, argumentation, and inquiry practices
target_learners: middle school students working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: STEM disciplinary practices such as modeling and argumentation
key_sources: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1

article_title: Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement
citation: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1
title: GDE observational rubric with five engagement dimensions
description: An observation rubric assessing a collaborative group's collective norms for engagement as multidimensional during shared activity. "The rubric encompasses five engagement dimensions using primarily 3-point quality rating scales, with disciplinary engagement specified using a 4-point scale (Rogat et al., 2022; Appendix A)." Ratings draw on members' behaviors, discourse, and nonverbal behaviors, with discourse as the primary data source; development included expert review and four preliminary trial rounds, and raters reached at least 0.67 Krippendorff alpha with a master rater.
requirements: Rater training with benchmark ratings and weekly coder drift checks; consensus rating by rater pairs after agreement declined
constraints: Metacognitive engagement ratings had 7% missing data due to the covert nature of metacognition; curriculum-specific indicators were developed for the disciplinary dimension
target_learners: middle school science and mathematics students
target_learning_goals: assessing quality of collaborative group engagement across behavioral, socioemotional, collaborative, metacognitive, and disciplinary dimensions
key_sources: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1

article_title: The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate
citation: Mohsen Alikhani & Esmaeil Bagheridoust. (2017). The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p44
title: GDOI treatment structured through Tuckman's four stages of group development
description: The treatment followed Tuckman's (1965) four stages of group development: Forming, Storming, Norming, and Performing, which the article says "have a great impact and relevance for the study of the classroom context". Over a 45-day semester with three 90-minute sessions per week, both groups received discussion topics from Four Corners 4; the experimental group worked with as much pair and group interaction as possible while the control group worked mostly individually.
requirements: A thirty-day period of time lapse before the post-test, with the semester lasting forty five days and classes meeting three times weekly for 90 minutes
constraints: The control group had no or little interaction with peers, performing mostly individually
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners aged 18-35 at a language institute
examples: Each session introduced a word list and grammar point, then a discussion question based on the unit title of Four Corners 4
key_sources: Mohsen Alikhani & Esmaeil Bagheridoust. (2017). The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p44

article_title: Comparing the impact of video feedback and group discussion on patient education performance among medical interns: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Managheb Seyed Esmaeil, Pouralimohamadi Neda, Taghipour Kaveh, Managheb Seyedeh Nastaran, Hosseini Hossein. (2025). Comparing the impact of video feedback and group discussion on patient education performance among medical interns: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07748-w
title: Group discussion workshop design: experience sharing, role-play, peer feedback, and instructor guidance
description: The GD intervention consisted of six two-hour interactive workshop sessions with four participants each. Sessions began with participants sharing patient education experiences, followed by a brief instructor presentation on essential patient education skills and role-playing exercises with observers providing peer feedback. The article states each session "comprised 15 min of scenario role-play by participants, followed by 15 min of group discussion and instructor feedback based on the patient-education feedback checklist", with participants rotating through roles across predesigned scenarios.
requirements: Instructor guidance using a patient-education feedback checklist
Predesigned scenarios with rotating participant roles
Same educational content as the VFB condition
constraints: The article notes group discussion efficacy can depend heavily on the facilitator's skills and the level of participant engagement
target_learning_goals: peer feedback and reflection on clinical communication
examples: Observers provided peer feedback after each role-play scenario, and the instructor offered guidance using the checklist
key_sources: Managheb Seyed Esmaeil, Pouralimohamadi Neda, Taghipour Kaveh, Managheb Seyedeh Nastaran, Hosseini Hossein. (2025). Comparing the impact of video feedback and group discussion on patient education performance among medical interns: a randomized controlled trial.
